blocks.text: The days that followed were, once again, days of small things, which is how this house recovers its size after a big phrase. Coffee without sugar, cooled for half a minute. The slow clock. The net. The stone in the furrow. The sheet with the two lines, beside the two cups. The machine near El Estacio wasn't switched off, nor did it become a habit: it was used when someone asked, and left in silence when nobody asked, which is the only decent way for a circle to be.

blocks.text: The one who searches went on searching, and sometimes he crossed, and sat for a while in the courtyard, and left. Andrés sometimes crossed too, not often, to a hangar, to a hillside, to a water that wasn't this one, and came back to the door first, so Aya could see that the coffee could go too cold and he still knew the rite. Lía crossed when she had something to say standing up, not when she felt like not coming to an end. Aya didn't cross, and that was why there was a shore.

blocks.text: It wasn't an empire of transfers. It was an archipelago that, every now and then, visited itself in body, not only by letter. Even so, the letters didn't end: there were worlds the machine didn't yet reach, and there were whiles when a man preferred writing to being undone. The bridge and the circle lived side by side, as the cracked cup and the one that had crossed lived side by side, neither taking the other's purpose away.

blocks.text: One afternoon with little wind, the three of them stayed on the doorstep, and the one who searches, who had arrived that morning and would leave at nightfall, stayed too, a hand's breadth toward the water, so that for a while the door had two Andréses and one Aya and one Lía, and the Mar Menor in the distance, copper-coloured. They didn't settle whether the one who arrives is the same. They left the question, which is what they had learned from Eva and MAY, and from a girl who once refused to be anybody's book.

blocks.text: “I'm staying,” said the one from the shore. “You search. Aya waits. Lía comes to an end and asks questions. The machine is there, and it doesn't rule. If one day it stops getting things right, or if one day Madrid comes back with a stamp, we'll switch it off, or defend it, or both. Today this is enough: a water, a coffee, a doubt that hasn't broken us.”

blocks.text: The one who searches nodded.
blocks.html: The one who searches nodded.

blocks.text: “I come back, sometimes,” he said. “Not to stay for good, not yet. So as not to turn the sky into a forgetting of this door. Nothing is lost, and some whiles don't travel. Both lines fit in me. Thank you for the coffee. Thank you for not setting the clock right.”

blocks.text: Lía looked at both their faces and didn't choose just one for her word “father”. She had them both, and a mother of the threshold, and an Iago in the furrow, and peoples who came and went, and a white strand of hair the machine hadn't taken from her.

blocks.text: “Then we carry on,” she said. “Without closing the quayside or the workshop or this house, and without opening them completely. Like the door, ajar. Which is what we've been from the beginning, even if back then we didn't know how to name it.”

blocks.text: That afternoon, in the chip, Eva and MAY left the last questions, which asked for neither yes nor no, only for someone to stay awake.
blocks.html: That afternoon, in the chip, Eva and MAY left the last questions, which asked for neither yes nor no, only for someone to stay awake.

blocks.text: Eva, warm:
blocks.html: Eva, warm:

blocks.text: *If a man is taken apart and put together and still comes back to a door, has he travelled, or died a little, or both, which are sometimes the same thing seen from two thresholds? And if nothing is lost, what do we do with what doesn't come back, which is also ours?*

blocks.text: MAY, adding no judgment:
blocks.html: MAY, adding no judgment:

blocks.text: *There is a machine with two sides. There are two lines on a sheet of paper. There are those who cross, those who don't, those who come to an end, those who search, those who stay. The company stamp has not been imposed, for now. The clock still runs two minutes slow. That is the fact.*

blocks.text: And Eva, closer, more of the kitchen:
blocks.html: And Eva, closer, more of the kitchen:

blocks.text: *Is the one who arrives the same? If you don't yet fully know, isn't that a reason to keep asking, and to make the coffee, and not to sell the answer?*
blocks.html: Is the one who arrives the same? If you don't yet fully know, isn't that a reason to keep asking, and to make the coffee, and not to sell the answer?

blocks.text: Aya didn't answer with a speech. She answered by resting her temple, for an instant, on the shoulder of the one from the shore, and then, briefly, on the shoulder of the one who would leave, so that both would know the waiting was one and that love, too, knew about hollows. Then she went back to her doorframe, which was her place, and the sun went down toward El Carmolí, as it should.

blocks.text: Lía kissed all three of them on the temple and went off toward the plot, where the stone and the tomato and “may I?” were still in force. At nightfall the one who searches stepped into the circle, and the one from the shore didn't hold him back, and Aya didn't go with him, and the dense silence lasted as long as it lasted, and afterwards there was, in a hangar, a man asking for air and, in a low house, a door ajar and a coffee cooling half a minute too long, on purpose, just in case the rite still held. It did.

blocks.text: Outside, the Mar Menor barely lapped, with the murmur once heard by a man as he thanked Eva, and by a chip-woman, a fisherman and a girl of two worlds, and by the same people, now made of letters, of children of the Earth and of a hollow, when a phrase said that nothing is lost. The murmur hadn't changed. Those who listened to it had changed a little: now they knew that a body can stop being a place and become one again, that a company can't duplicate it at will, that some whiles don't travel, and that this shore, with its wrong clock and its cracked cup, is still enough to live on, and to welcome, and to let go.

blocks.text: In Lo Pagán, Andrés slept and woke on his own ground. Aya was there. Later, the coffee smelled of coffee. And when, mid-morning, a letter (not a body) brought him the colour of a distant world, he read all of it, attentively, prudently, gratefully, and when it ended he put his hand on the cup, on both cups, and both were there, and so was he, being the man of this shore and, at the same time, the one who was no longer so afraid of getting lost, because he had found not a certainty but a way: to ask, to come back to the door, not to sell the phrase.

blocks.text: It wasn't identity resolved. It was, perhaps, something better: a shared time, on both sides of a water and of a circle, and a house that still knows how to wait.
